Hi — I've been building Lean4 to WASM for a production use case (compiling a Lean Effect Interpreter module to a browser-delivered WASM binary via Emscripten) and independently found fixes for two issues I'd like to contribute upstream if the team would welcome PRs:

  1. Issue #6817 — libleanrt.a for linux_wasm32 contains unresolved references to uv_strerror, uv_os_tmpdir, uv_fs_mkstemp, and uv_fs_mkdtemp even with LEAN_EMSCRIPTEN defined. The fix is adding #ifndef LEAN_EMSCRIPTEN guards in src/runtime/io.cpp, following the same pattern already applied in src/runtime/uv/dns.cpp (PR #9258). I've been running an equivalent patch in production since v4.27.0 — it works.
  2. unique_lock::release() missing from single-thread stub — When building with -DMULTI_THREAD=OFF (required for Emscripten), the stub unique_lock<T> in src/runtime/thread.h is missing a release() method that the runtime calls. Adding T* release() { return nullptr; } fixes the compile error. This doesn't appear to be documented anywhere publicly.
    Would PRs for these be welcome? Happy to align on the preferred approach (macro scope, etc.) before writing the diffs.
Hi, I was just wondering if you are planning to release your WASM build to the public or is it proprietary? Just so I know if I should try my own build or not?

Mr Proof said:

Hi, I was just wondering if you are planning to release your WASM build to the public or is it proprietary? Just so I know if I should try my own build or not?

Nice to meet you Mr Proof. Short answer is I'm a noob and self-conscious, but extremely motivated and deeply curious. I haven't been active in the past in OSS projects but I think I'll be trying to get this to a point I'm willing to release it.

So, yes, I am planning to release the WASM build and my larger product to the public, and I yearn for collaboration. I think I'd like to wait a week or two to clean up my mess beforehand though.

I'm not part of the core team, so I can't comment on whether PRs are welcome for these issues, but I just want to add that I would love to have an (official) WASM build for educational settings. (Not having to install on students machines or manage a server would be great)

Do you have any indication of the speed of the WASM build you're running vs running the native version? Are you doing anything with Mathlib in your project?

Thanks for the interest, Pim! I'll do my best to answer based on my understanding, feel free to correct me / ask for clarifications:

Current state:

On speed: once the binary is loaded, each EI command takes roughly 0.05–0.11 ms total round-trip — essentially instantaneous. The interesting part is that the pure Lean evaluation inside the binary is sub-microsecond (we're talking 0.4–1.6 µs per command), so nearly all of the round-trip cost is actually JSON marshaling at the JS↔WASM boundary, not the Lean computation itself.

The cold-start cost is about 500 ms for the first request after page load — that covers binary fetch, Emscripten init, and Lean runtime initialization. That's the number that matters most for a classroom setting, since everything after that is sub-millisecond. Streaming instantiation and an IndexedDB module cache would bring that down significantly on repeat loads.

On Mathlib: no, explicitly excluded by design. The binary is 9.3 MB precisely because it doesn't carry the parser, elaborator, or Mathlib — just the EI evaluation layer. Adding any of those would push it toward 100 MB, which is the situation the broader community is stuck in.

I'm planning to open-source the build infrastructure (scripts, runtime patches, stub files) in the next few weeks if there's a demand.

I'm not completely certain this informtaion is correct, but as far as I remember the current state of wasm builds is: @Alexander Bentkamp once put in quite some effort in getting wasm to work initially after which it got included into the lean4 repo but turned out to be unmaintainable with the amount of resources the FRO is willing to allocate to this wasm topic (which is basically zero, and that's completely reasonable imo).

So I would assume that a RFC fixing the wasm build would be welcome if it is reviewable and doesn't put any new maintenance burden on the FRO. But I'm not affiliated with them, so this is purely an estimate.

Otherwise, like you suggest, providing your own repo with this solution might be the easiest. I think you can even ask for it to be moved under leanprover-community if you intend to maintain the project going forth.

I'm not a lean4 core dev, just a C++ programmer, so take my opinion with a grain of salt. But both of these seem like reasonable changes to PR: they are just fixing particular build configurations not adding complicated features. Your second suggestion (unique_lock) seems like a totally uncontroversial change and the first also seems reasonable given that we already use the #ifndef LEAN_EMSCRIPTEN pattern.
@Keith Seim I'm the relevant person for the component that's affected by #2, feel free to make the PR.
and just noticed for the first issue that lean4#6817 has the PR-welcome tag

Thanks everyone for the responses — sorry for the delay getting back.

PRs: Both fixes are up:

  • unique_lock::release() stub: lean4#13297
  • libuv symbol leakage (#6817): lean4#13298

@Henrik Böving — thank you for the green light on the thread.h change.

Project update: Since my original post, I've completed a migration away from the WASM browser runtime. The browser now runs a code-generated TypeScript effects interpreter whose evaluators are generated directly from the Lean specification, with structural isomorphism witnesses (Lean proofs that the generated TS types mirror the Lean source types) and a conformance test suite comparing Lean subprocess output against generated TypeScript. The Lean EI remains the authoritative server-side runtime.

Why we moved off WASM (before/after comparison)

Dimension WASM (before) Verified TS (after)
Build time 3–6 min cold; 8–10 min on protocol changes <5s incremental codegen
Browser cold start 2–5s (9.3 MB binary compile + init) Zero (TS parsed by V8 JIT)
Bundle size 9.3 MB WASM + 66 KB loader + .gen.ts ~200 KB bundled .gen.ts only
Hot-path latency 1–10ms (JSON across WASM boundary) ~0ms (sync, native JS objects)
Patch maintenance 8 patched runtime files per Lean bump Zero patches — codegen only
Offline Requires cached WASM binary Always available

The core issue was the serialization boundary tax: every WASM call required JSON encode → malloc → ccall → free → JSON decode. Benchmarks showed the boundary cost was 50–100x the actual Lean computation (0.04–0.11ms FFI round-trip vs 0.4–1.6μs compute). The Prisma project saw the same pattern moving from Rust binary to TypeScript (3.4x faster after eliminating the boundary). Even with WASM, the browser still needed generated TypeScript for instant synchronous feedback (field change evaluation, constraint display), so we were maintaining two parallel browser runtimes. The verified TS approach collapses these into one.

That said, the upstream fixes remain valuable for anyone building Lean to WASM — the libuv symbol leakage affects the official linux_wasm32 artifact regardless of what downstream projects do with it.

@Pim Otte — re: educational use, our WASM build was specific to a single Lean module (an entity interpreter, ~10 commands), not the full elaborator/parser. A general-purpose educational WASM build would be a larger undertaking, but the runtime patches we're upstreaming should help anyone attempting it. We didn't use Mathlib. Re: speed, the narrow-scope WASM binary was roughly 3–6 min cold build vs <30s for the native binary — manageable for CI but not for interactive development.

@Mr Proof — the WASM binary itself is specific to our application (it embeds a particular Lean module), but the build process and patches are general-purpose. Once the PRs land, the main blockers to building any Lean module to WASM will be significantly reduced. Happy to share the build script structure if that's useful.
